sourceTitle: When a Probability Becomes a Headline
scoreRule: 1 point per correct MC item; 10 points maximum; local provisional grade only
description: EN/C2 independently authored Asteroids test: uncertainty, evidence and planetary-defence reasoning. Human content review pending.

tabs.title: Interpreting the evidence
tabs.description: Read between the lines and establish the main argument.

tabs.title: Evidence in practice
tabs.description: Transfer scientific reasoning to new situations.

questions.q: What is obscured by the metaphor of humanity fighting a hostile universe?
choices: The fact that asteroid orbits are impossible to study scientifically.
The slower, evidence-dependent work that makes a proportionate response possible.
The historical frequency of every asteroid collision.
The reasons that scientists use telescopes instead of spacecraft.
questions.explanation: The opening challenges dramatic conflict framing because it conceals sustained observation and interpretation.

questions.q: What is the strongest implication of the observation that 'precision and completeness are not synonyms'?
choices: Precise measurements are meaningless unless every object is visible.
Completeness can be calculated directly from a single telescope image.
Infrared instruments provide no additional information about dark objects.
Accurate estimates about detected objects may still omit populations surveys fail to observe.
questions.explanation: The writer distinguishes precision about known orbits from catalogue selection effects.

questions.q: Why does the Apophis episode illustrate a problem beyond a mistaken early prediction?
choices: The asteroid's orbit changed abruptly after a human intervention.
Radar observations contradicted basic physical laws.
A preliminary warning later became a scientific opportunity through revised evidence.
The original media coverage accurately anticipated how astronomers would respond in 2029.
questions.explanation: Apophis shifted from apparent threat to valuable close approach as improved data excluded impact.

questions.q: What is the force of the description of DART as an 'instructive counterpoint'?
choices: The experiment demonstrates an evidence-based, conditional method rather than a cinematic universal shield.
It establishes that a kinetic impact must always be the preferred response.
It shows that dramatic emergency intervention is more reliable than early warning.
It replaces the need for orbit modelling with direct spacecraft observations.
questions.explanation: The DART paragraph uses an actual but limited deflection to counter theatrical assumptions.

questions.q: Why does the writer call apparently rising risk estimates a possible sign of responsible reasoning?
choices: The early estimates are selected to maximise public concern.
They reflect updates to a model as available orbital solutions are constrained.
Scientific institutions require risk to rise before they can act.
The object's actual path changes whenever its probability is recalculated.
questions.explanation: Revisions are part of evidence-based narrowing of uncertainty, not necessarily institutional indecision.

questions.q: What does the distinction between experimental evidence and a 'universal shield' emphasise?
choices: One mission is sufficient only if every asteroid has the same orbit.
Experiments cannot meaningfully inform decisions about genuine threats.
The effect of an impact depends on conditions that a single mission cannot exhaustively test.
Detection can be abandoned once kinetic deflection has been demonstrated.
questions.explanation: The text stresses the conditionality of outcomes across composition, structure, warning and verification.

questions.q: Why does the conclusion prefer systems that can withstand correction to reassuring declarations?
choices: Scientific credibility requires all uncertainty to be eliminated in advance.
Such systems avoid the need for political decisions under uncertainty.
An institution proves authority by never changing its forecasts.
Public trust is better supported by inspectable assumptions and revisable decisions.
questions.explanation: The conclusion explicitly defines authority through transparent evidence and openness to correction.

questions.q: A government presents a precise risk percentage but omits its observational selection effects. What is the key danger?
choices: The estimate cannot possibly reflect a real asteroid's trajectory.
The audience may confuse numerical accuracy about detected objects with complete knowledge of hazards.
The percentage becomes impossible to communicate in ordinary language.
The instruments will automatically stop detecting dim asteroids.
questions.explanation: The author warns that a precise catalogue statistic can conceal which objects are difficult to detect.

questions.q: Two public messages follow a changed orbit estimate. Which is more defensible?
choices: Explain what new measurements changed and which assumptions remain uncertain.
Insist the original estimate was certain to prevent public confusion.
Avoid mentioning the revision until all future observations are complete.
Present the change as evidence that no asteroid risk deserves attention.
questions.explanation: The writer favours open revision and explanation of assumptions over false certainty.

questions.q: A proposed defence plan uses DART as proof that late interventions always work. What is the strongest rebuttal?
choices: The spacecraft never measurably changed Dimorphos's orbit.
A collision with Dimorphos was legally impossible to arrange.
An asteroid's distance from the Sun alone determines whether deflection succeeds.
A modest early change may matter more than a dramatic last-minute attempt, depending on the target.
questions.explanation: The article directly contrasts early measured deflection with late theatrical interventions and emphasises conditional efficacy.
